newsitem.title: UK: Britain tells EU to tighten up on beef safety.
newsitem.headline: Britain tells EU to tighten up on beef safety.

text.p: Britain may ban beef imports from the European Union unless controls on mad cow disease are tightened up right across the EU, Agriculture Minister Jack Cunningham said on Thursday.
He said the present legal requirements for the head, spinal cord and certain other tissues of cattle to be removed from the food chain applied only to animals slaughtered in Britain.

"The government is opening consultation on proposals which would mean that the requirement to remove and dispose of specified tissues would apply not only to such carcasses but also to bovine material which has been imported into Britain," he said in a written parliamentary answer.
He said it was ridiculous that beef, reared in Europe, was on sale in Britain but did not meet its tough safety rules.

The EU banned British beef and beef products more than a year ago when the previous Conservative government admitted a possible link between bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease) which is a deadly brain disease, and its human equivalent, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

Cunningham also announced plans for the compulsory slaughter of sheep infected with scrapie although he insisted there was no new scientific evidence to suggest a link between BSE and scrapie, a similar brain-wasting disease.

"The government's intention is to reinforce the existing legal requirement on farmers to notify all cases of scrapie by providing new powers for the compulsory slaughter of affected animals, with payment of compensation, and by initiating a survey of brains from abattoirs and a postal survey of farms," he said.
It was a precautionary measure, he said, adding that the findings of that survey will be published.
Cunningham said the EU had dragged its feet over scrapie too.

"During the latter part of 1996...the Commission proposed EU-wide controls on the use of spleen of all sheep and the brain and spinal cord of sheep which were more than a year old. Unfortunately, despite support from the United Kingdom and a few other countries, the majority of member states rejected this proposal."
